evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: Intangible costs (pain and suffering) were explicitly excluded from the cost calculations.
Public health surveillance and administration costs were not incorporated into the economic impact estimate.
Costs incurred by a patient beyond the 1997-2000 study period (e.g., ongoing late-sequelae care) were not captured; the authors flag this as a source of underestimation.

The document cites another study (Steer et al.) finding that approximately 7% of LD cases remained asymptomatic within a 20-month period and notes these patients may have costs beyond the study window, but this percentage is from a different cited study, not the document's own measurement, and no cost figure is attached to it here.
Patient household income was collected via the appendix questionnaire (categorical bands) but no income-stratified cost analysis is reported in the main results.

The questionnaire asked whether family members helped with housework/childcare, but costs were only quantified when the patient paid for that help; unpaid caregiving time itself was not monetarily valued.

Extensive tick-exposure and personal-protective-behavior data (occupation, outdoor exposure, yard/landscape type, pet contact, protective clothing, repellent use) were collected in the appendix questionnaire for risk-factor purposes but are not tied to any quantified cost figure in the results reported here.
evidence_gaps: Longitudinal or lifetime cost data beyond the 1997-2000 observation window would be needed to quantify the 'longterm sequelae' the authors describe as 'debilitating to patients and costly to society' but did not themselves measure past the study period.
A method for valuing intangible costs (pain and suffering) would be needed to complete the societal-perspective total the authors otherwise used.

A nationally representative cost sample matched to the CDC's 2002 surveillance case-mix (rather than a single region's clinical-case-definition cohort) would be needed to validate the ~$203 million nationwide extrapolation.

Cost breakdowns by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or insurance type are not reported; only sex was tested, and only for direct medical costs via regression (finding no significant difference), not for the total societal cost figures.

A higher-response-rate survey (actual response was ~22%, with indirect/nonmedical/productivity cost data drawn from only ~8% of all identified patients and restricted to 1997-1998) would reduce extrapolation uncertainty underlying the nonmedical and productivity-loss cost components.
comparison_boundaries: Direct medical costs were abstracted from medical records/charges across all 4 study years (1997-2000), while indirect medical costs, nonmedical costs, and productivity losses came only from patient questionnaires restricted to 1997-1998; the combined per-patient total-cost figures ($1,965 mean / $281 median) therefore blend a 4-year direct-cost sample with a 2-year indirect-cost sample and should not be treated as measured over an identical time window.

The mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total-cost figures diverge sharply because a small number of high-cost (mostly late-stage) patients drive the mean; the authors themselves caution that 'using mean cost to estimate national impact could be an overestimation' - these are two different central-tendency measures of a skewed distribution and should not be averaged or pooled into a single number.

The regional Maryland Eastern Shore cohort (3,415 LD-relevant patients identified via a clinical case definition, which the authors say 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases') must not be pooled with the nationwide $203 million (2002 dollars) extrapolation, which instead scales the regional per-case cost to the CDC's surveillance-case-definition count of 23,763 national cases in 2002 - the two populations use different case definitions, different sizes, and different years.

Per-stage cohort mean direct medical costs (e.g., $1,609 vs. $4,240 in 1997) are simple group means; the regression-based '50%/100% higher' relative-cost findings come from a separate log-transformed OLS model controlling for other covariates (hospitalization, serology, therapy, consultation, cohort year, sex, age) and should not be directly summed with or substituted for the raw per-stage mean/median dollar figures.

All medical-cost figures are already converted to year-2000 dollars via the medical-care CPI, and nonmedical/productivity-loss figures via the general CPI; the nationwide $203 million estimate is explicitly stated in 2002 dollars and must not be combined with the year-2000-dollar regional figures without separate deflation/inflation adjustment.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Using multivariate (OLS) regression on direct medical costs controlling for diagnosis group, procedures, cohort year, and patient characteristics including sex and age, the study found 'no cost difference...seen between men and women' in direct medical costs per LD patient.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The regional Maryland Eastern Shore cost figures (e.g., the $1,965 mean / $281 median per-patient totals, and stage-specific costs) were derived from patients identified via 'a final diagnosis code in their medical records' and direct-medical-cost charge data from a managed-care organization (Delmarva Health Plan) and office-based physician records (Methods, p.654) - a diagnosis-code/claims-type identification method. The document itself separately acknowledges that its clinical (rather than surveillance) case definition 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases,' and that national surveillance-based case counts 'are believed to be underreported' - reflecting the same kind of coding/definition-driven count uncertainty this caveat flags, though the document attributes its own local count issue to case-definition choice rather than ICD-10 coding granularity specifically.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The expected mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total cost per LD patient, the combined per-patient direct-medical ($2,970) plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity ($5,202) costs, and the nationwide extrapolated economic impact (~$203 million) are all presented as single pooled figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status. Sex was examined only for the direct-medical-cost regression (finding no difference), not for these total societal cost figures, and age was included only as a regression covariate, not reported as a stratified cost breakdown.

decision_relevance.summary: This 2006 CDC-authored peer-reviewed study and its appended patient cost questionnaire provide a field-collected, multi-component (direct medical, indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss) cost estimate for Lyme disease in one U.S. endemic region, broken out by disease stage. A simulator built on it could let patients/advocates, clinicians/care-delivery teams, and payers/policymakers explore how documented per-patient costs differ between early- and late-stage disease, how skewed (mean vs. median) the cost distribution is, and how a regional per-case cost might be scaled - with explicit caveats about case-definition and extrapolation uncertainty - to a national reported case count. It cannot support any Long COVID modeling, lifetime/chronic post-treatment cost estimation beyond the 1997-2000 window, or cost breakdowns by age, race, disability, or other protected subgroup categories, since the document does not provide these.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could use the stage-specific median and mean cost figures (e.g., $397 median for early-stage vs. $923 median for late-stage LD, 2000 dollars) to illustrate how documented out-of-pocket and productivity costs differ when diagnosis/treatment occurs at an earlier vs. later disease stage in this cohort.

Payers/policymakers could use the combined per-patient direct medical cost ($2,970) plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost ($5,202) figures, scaled against a selectable annual reported Lyme case count, to produce an order-of-magnitude cost projection - while the simulator must flag that the $203 million national figure in the source document is an extrapolation from one regional, clinically defined cohort, not a nationally representative claims- or surveillance-matched estimate.

contextual_issues: Intangible costs (pain and suffering) were explicitly excluded from the cost calculations.
Public health surveillance and administration costs were not incorporated into the economic impact estimate.
Costs incurred by a patient beyond the 1997-2000 study period (e.g., ongoing late-sequelae care) were not captured; the authors flag this as a source of underestimation.

The document cites another study (Steer et al.) finding that approximately 7% of LD cases remained asymptomatic within a 20-month period and notes these patients may have costs beyond the study window, but this percentage is from a different cited study, not the document's own measurement, and no cost figure is attached to it here.
Patient household income was collected via the appendix questionnaire (categorical bands) but no income-stratified cost analysis is reported in the main results.

The questionnaire asked whether family members helped with housework/childcare, but costs were only quantified when the patient paid for that help; unpaid caregiving time itself was not monetarily valued.

Extensive tick-exposure and personal-protective-behavior data (occupation, outdoor exposure, yard/landscape type, pet contact, protective clothing, repellent use) were collected in the appendix questionnaire for risk-factor purposes but are not tied to any quantified cost figure in the results reported here.
evidence_gaps: Longitudinal or lifetime cost data beyond the 1997-2000 observation window would be needed to quantify the 'longterm sequelae' the authors describe as 'debilitating to patients and costly to society' but did not themselves measure past the study period.
A method for valuing intangible costs (pain and suffering) would be needed to complete the societal-perspective total the authors otherwise used.

A nationally representative cost sample matched to the CDC's 2002 surveillance case-mix (rather than a single region's clinical-case-definition cohort) would be needed to validate the ~$203 million nationwide extrapolation.

Cost breakdowns by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or insurance type are not reported; only sex was tested, and only for direct medical costs via regression (finding no significant difference), not for the total societal cost figures.

A higher-response-rate survey (actual response was ~22%, with indirect/nonmedical/productivity cost data drawn from only ~8% of all identified patients and restricted to 1997-1998) would reduce extrapolation uncertainty underlying the nonmedical and productivity-loss cost components.
comparison_boundaries: Direct medical costs were abstracted from medical records/charges across all 4 study years (1997-2000), while indirect medical costs, nonmedical costs, and productivity losses came only from patient questionnaires restricted to 1997-1998; the combined per-patient total-cost figures ($1,965 mean / $281 median) therefore blend a 4-year direct-cost sample with a 2-year indirect-cost sample and should not be treated as measured over an identical time window.

The mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total-cost figures diverge sharply because a small number of high-cost (mostly late-stage) patients drive the mean; the authors themselves caution that 'using mean cost to estimate national impact could be an overestimation' - these are two different central-tendency measures of a skewed distribution and should not be averaged or pooled into a single number.

The regional Maryland Eastern Shore cohort (3,415 LD-relevant patients identified via a clinical case definition, which the authors say 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases') must not be pooled with the nationwide $203 million (2002 dollars) extrapolation, which instead scales the regional per-case cost to the CDC's surveillance-case-definition count of 23,763 national cases in 2002 - the two populations use different case definitions, different sizes, and different years.

Per-stage cohort mean direct medical costs (e.g., $1,609 vs. $4,240 in 1997) are simple group means; the regression-based '50%/100% higher' relative-cost findings come from a separate log-transformed OLS model controlling for other covariates (hospitalization, serology, therapy, consultation, cohort year, sex, age) and should not be directly summed with or substituted for the raw per-stage mean/median dollar figures.

All medical-cost figures are already converted to year-2000 dollars via the medical-care CPI, and nonmedical/productivity-loss figures via the general CPI; the nationwide $203 million estimate is explicitly stated in 2002 dollars and must not be combined with the year-2000-dollar regional figures without separate deflation/inflation adjustment.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Using multivariate (OLS) regression on direct medical costs controlling for diagnosis group, procedures, cohort year, and patient characteristics including sex and age, the study found 'no cost difference...seen between men and women' in direct medical costs per LD patient.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The regional Maryland Eastern Shore cost figures (e.g., the $1,965 mean / $281 median per-patient totals, and stage-specific costs) were derived from patients identified via 'a final diagnosis code in their medical records' and direct-medical-cost charge data from a managed-care organization (Delmarva Health Plan) and office-based physician records (Methods, p.654) - a diagnosis-code/claims-type identification method. The document itself separately acknowledges that its clinical (rather than surveillance) case definition 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases,' and that national surveillance-based case counts 'are believed to be underreported' - reflecting the same kind of coding/definition-driven count uncertainty this caveat flags, though the document attributes its own local count issue to case-definition choice rather than ICD-10 coding granularity specifically.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The expected mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total cost per LD patient, the combined per-patient direct-medical ($2,970) plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity ($5,202) costs, and the nationwide extrapolated economic impact (~$203 million) are all presented as single pooled figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status. Sex was examined only for the direct-medical-cost regression (finding no difference), not for these total societal cost figures, and age was included only as a regression covariate, not reported as a stratified cost breakdown.

decision_relevance.summary: This 2006 CDC-authored peer-reviewed study and its appended patient cost questionnaire provide a field-collected, multi-component (direct medical, indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss) cost estimate for Lyme disease in one U.S. endemic region, broken out by disease stage. A simulator built on it could let patients/advocates, clinicians/care-delivery teams, and payers/policymakers explore how documented per-patient costs differ between early- and late-stage disease, how skewed (mean vs. median) the cost distribution is, and how a regional per-case cost might be scaled - with explicit caveats about case-definition and extrapolation uncertainty - to a national reported case count. It cannot support any Long COVID modeling, lifetime/chronic post-treatment cost estimation beyond the 1997-2000 window, or cost breakdowns by age, race, disability, or other protected subgroup categories, since the document does not provide these.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could use the stage-specific median and mean cost figures (e.g., $397 median for early-stage vs. $923 median for late-stage LD, 2000 dollars) to illustrate how documented out-of-pocket and productivity costs differ when diagnosis/treatment occurs at an earlier vs. later disease stage in this cohort.

Payers/policymakers could use the combined per-patient direct medical cost ($2,970) plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost ($5,202) figures, scaled against a selectable annual reported Lyme case count, to produce an order-of-magnitude cost projection - while the simulator must flag that the $203 million national figure in the source document is an extrapolation from one regional, clinically defined cohort, not a nationally representative claims- or surveillance-matched estimate.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Cost Burden Explorer (Zhang et al. 2006, Maryland Eastern Shore)
spec.boundary: This simulation represents direct medical, indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs documented for one Maryland Eastern Shore cohort of Lyme disease (LD) patients, 1997-2000, as reported in a peer-reviewed CDC-authored study. It omits costs beyond the 2000 study window, intangible pain-and-suffering costs, public-health surveillance/administration costs, and any breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability, or income (the document did not report these). The nationwide projection is an illustrative scaling exercise, not a validated national estimate.

takeaway.patient: In this Maryland Eastern Shore study, patients whose Lyme disease was documented at a late stage had much higher direct medical costs in the same year than those documented at an early stage ($4,240 vs $1,609 in the 1997 group). Across all patients in the study, the 'typical' (median) total cost was much lower than the 'average' (mean) cost, because a small number of late-stage patients with very high costs pulled the average up - so an average figure alone can overstate what a typical patient experienced.
takeaway.care: This dataset shows a large, consistent gap between early- and late-stage direct medical costs within the same cohort-year, and separately documents meaningful nonmedical (travel, paid help) and productivity-loss costs that are easy to miss if only medical-record charges are tracked. The cost figures also mix a case count built from clinical diagnosis codes with a national count built from a surveillance case definition - the study's authors note their own clinical definition may have captured more cases than the surveillance definition would.
takeaway.policy: Scaling this cohort's per-patient combined cost to a national reported Lyme disease case count produces an order-of-magnitude estimate in the hundreds of millions of dollars per year, close to the study's own reported ~$203 million (2002 dollars) estimate, though this computed value will not exactly match because of a price-year/case-definition gap the document does not fully resolve. The study's authors themselves caution that using mean rather than median cost, and using a clinical rather than surveillance case count, both push this projection toward overestimation of a 'typical' case burden - while nationally reported surveillance counts are also believed to undercount true LD incidence, pulling in the opposite direction.

patient: If you or a family member have been diagnosed with Lyme disease, it may be worth asking your clinician whether your diagnosis stage (early vs. late) is linked to the cost differences this kind of study reports, to set realistic expectations for care and expenses.
Consider tracking nonmedical costs (travel to appointments, paid help at home) separately from medical bills, since this study found those added meaningfully to total burden but are easy to overlook.

When you see an 'average' cost figure for a condition like this, consider asking what the 'typical' (median) cost looks like too - this study found the two numbers can differ enormously because a few very costly cases skew the average upward.
This dataset reflects one region studied over 1997-2000; use it only as a general illustration of the early-vs-late-stage cost pattern, not as a prediction of your own specific costs today.
care: Given the documented cost gap between early- and late-stage direct medical costs in the same cohort-year, this finding may be worth checking against your own practice's time-to-diagnosis and staging patterns.

Because the study found that indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost data came from a small, time-limited patient subset, consider whether your own program has a way to capture these costs more completely for patients you see.

The gap between a clinical case-definition count and a surveillance case-definition count noted in this study may be worth reviewing against how your own setting documents and codes Lyme disease diagnoses, since the two counts are not interchangeable.

The study found no significant sex-based difference in direct medical costs; consider whether this is consistent with patterns in your own patient population before assuming cost drivers differ by sex.
policy: Use the adjustable national case count alongside the combined per-patient cost to generate a range of order-of-magnitude national burden estimates for planning purposes, rather than treating the single $203 million figure as precise.

When comparing this cohort's mean versus median per-patient costs, favor the median for 'typical patient' budgeting scenarios and reserve the mean for total-burden projections, consistent with the study authors' own caution about mean-based overestimation.

Treat the national case count used in any scaled projection as a surveillance-based figure that the cited literature suggests likely undercounts true Lyme disease incidence, and the regional cohort's clinical case definition as potentially overcounting cases relative to that surveillance definition - both uncertainties should be flagged together in any budget estimate.

Consider that this pooled cost estimate has not been examined for variation by age, race/ethnicity, or income, and that disaggregated federal survey data (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) could help assess whether this pattern holds across subgroups before using it for targeted policy design.

package.documentation:
## Source
Zhang et al., 'Economic Impact of Lyme Disease,' *Emerging Infectious Diseases*, 2006 (CDC-authored), Maryland Eastern Shore, 1997-2000, with an appended patient cost/risk questionnaire.

## What the inputs represent
Early- and late-stage direct medical cost inputs are the document's own 1997-cohort means (Results, p.657). The combined direct-medical and combined indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost inputs are the document's own per-patient averages, derived from annual aggregate totals divided by patient counts (Discussion, p.658). The national case count (23,763, year 2002) is the CDC surveillance figure the document itself used for its nationwide extrapolation (Introduction, p.653). Mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total-cost inputs are the document's own pooled figures across all five diagnosis groups (Results, p.657, Figure 3). All dollar figures are in 2000 dollars except the national case count (2002) and the illustrative nationwide output, which mixes both years without a reproducible conversion step.

## Key limitations
The regional cost figures were identified from medical-record diagnosis codes and managed-care/physician charge data; the document itself notes its clinical case definition 'may have overestimated' local case counts, while national surveillance-based counts are separately believed to undercount true Lyme disease incidence - these are two distinct count issues the document does not combine. The pooled mean/median/combined cost figures are presented without breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability, or income; only sex was tested (via regression on direct medical costs), finding no significant difference - federal survey data sources such as MEPS, NHIS, and BRFSS generally support more disaggregated analysis than this document performed. Indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost data came from only ~8% of all identified patients, restricted to 1997-1998, with a ~22% survey response rate. Intangible costs (pain and suffering) and costs beyond 2000 were excluded. The nationwide $203 million figure is a one-region extrapolation, not a nationally representative estimate, and should be treated as illustrative order-of-magnitude only.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

takeaway.policy: Scaling this cohort's per-patient combined cost to a national reported Lyme disease case count produces an order-of-magnitude estimate in the hundreds of millions of dollars per year, close to the study's own reported ~$203 million (2002 dollars) estimate, though this computed value will not exactly match because of a price-year/case-definition gap the document does not fully resolve. The study's authors themselves caution that using mean rather than median cost, and using a clinical rather than surveillance case count, both push this projection toward overestimation of a 'typical' case burden - while nationally reported surveillance counts are also believed to undercount true LD incidence, pulling in the opposite direction.

patient: If you or a family member have been diagnosed with Lyme disease, it may be worth asking your clinician whether your diagnosis stage (early vs. late) is linked to the cost differences this kind of study reports, to set realistic expectations for care and expenses.
Consider tracking nonmedical costs (travel to appointments, paid help at home) separately from medical bills, since this study found those added meaningfully to total burden but are easy to overlook.

When you see an 'average' cost figure for a condition like this, consider asking what the 'typical' (median) cost looks like too - this study found the two numbers can differ enormously because a few very costly cases skew the average upward.
This dataset reflects one region studied over 1997-2000; use it only as a general illustration of the early-vs-late-stage cost pattern, not as a prediction of your own specific costs today.
care: Given the documented cost gap between early- and late-stage direct medical costs in the same cohort-year, this finding may be worth checking against your own practice's time-to-diagnosis and staging patterns.

Because the study found that indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost data came from a small, time-limited patient subset, consider whether your own program has a way to capture these costs more completely for patients you see.

The gap between a clinical case-definition count and a surveillance case-definition count noted in this study may be worth reviewing against how your own setting documents and codes Lyme disease diagnoses, since the two counts are not interchangeable.

The study found no significant sex-based difference in direct medical costs; consider whether this is consistent with patterns in your own patient population before assuming cost drivers differ by sex.
policy: Use the adjustable national case count alongside the combined per-patient cost to generate a range of order-of-magnitude national burden estimates for planning purposes, rather than treating the single $203 million figure as precise.

When comparing this cohort's mean versus median per-patient costs, favor the median for 'typical patient' budgeting scenarios and reserve the mean for total-burden projections, consistent with the study authors' own caution about mean-based overestimation.

Treat the national case count used in any scaled projection as a surveillance-based figure that the cited literature suggests likely undercounts true Lyme disease incidence, and the regional cohort's clinical case definition as potentially overcounting cases relative to that surveillance definition - both uncertainties should be flagged together in any budget estimate.

Consider that this pooled cost estimate has not been examined for variation by age, race/ethnicity, or income, and that disaggregated federal survey data (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) could help assess whether this pattern holds across subgroups before using it for targeted policy design.

inputs.interpretation: This is the mean direct medical cost the document reports for clinically defined early-stage LD patients in the 1997 cohort; moving it tests how sensitive the early-vs-late cost gap below is to this specific cohort-year figure.

inputs.label: Late-stage direct medical cost per patient, 1997 cohort
inputs.source: Results, p.657; default is the document's own reported 1997-cohort mean; 3500-5000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the mean direct medical cost the document reports for clinically defined late-stage LD patients in the 1997 cohort; it is the main driver of the large documented stage-based cost gap.

inputs.label: Combined direct medical cost per patient (early/late-stage)
inputs.source: Discussion, p.658 (derived by the document from $1,455,081 total charges across 490 cases); 2000-4000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own per-patient average of annual aggregate direct medical charges across early- and late-stage patients; it feeds into the combined and nationwide cost outputs below.

inputs.label: Combined indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost per patient
inputs.source: Discussion, p.658 (derived by the document from $436,949 total across 84 survey-responding cases); 3000-7000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own per-patient average of indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs drawn from the survey subset; raising or lowering it tests how much this non-medical-record component contributes to total per-patient and nationwide cost estimates.

inputs.label: National LD cases reported to CDC
inputs.source: Introduction, p.653 (2002 reported case count); 15000-35000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the CDC surveillance-case-definition count the document used to scale regional costs nationally; varying it shows how sensitive the nationwide projection is to the reported case count, independent of any true-incidence uncertainty.

inputs.label: Mean total cost per patient, all diagnosis groups
inputs.source: Results, p.657, Figure 3; 1000-3000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own pooled average total cost across all five diagnosis groups; compare it to the median input below to see how much a few high-cost patients inflate the average.

inputs.label: Median total cost per patient, all diagnosis groups
inputs.source: Abstract; Results, p.657, Figure 3; 100-500 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own pooled typical (median) total cost across all five diagnosis groups; it represents what a more typical patient experienced, unlike the mean which is pulled upward by costly late-stage cases.

outputs.label: Late-stage minus early-stage direct medical cost, 1997 cohort (positive = late-stage costs more; cannot be negative given the chosen input ranges)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between typical direct medical costs for late-stage versus early-stage Lyme disease patients in the same 1997 cohort. The document reports late-stage costs were substantially higher that year; a larger gap here reflects a bigger documented difference in medical treatment cost by disease stage at diagnosis, not a measure of delay in reaching diagnosis itself.

outputs.label: Combined direct medical plus indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost per patient
outputs.interpretation: This adds the document's own derived direct medical cost per patient to its derived indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost per patient for early- and late-stage patients combined. At document defaults this totals $8,172, which does not match the document's separately reported overall mean ($1,965) or median ($281) cost per patient across all five diagnosis groups (including suspected LD, tick-bite-only, and other complaints); those are different, broader-population figures and the document does not reconcile the two.

outputs.label: Mean minus median total cost per patient, all diagnosis groups (positive = distribution is right-skewed by a small number of high-cost patients; cannot be negative given the chosen input ranges, consistent with the document's reported values)
outputs.interpretation: This shows how far the pooled average (mean) total cost exceeds the pooled typical (median) total cost. The document explicitly attributes this gap to a small number of costly late-stage patients and cautions that using the mean to project national costs could overestimate the typical patient's burden.

outputs.label: Projected nationwide annual economic impact of LD and related complaints (illustrative extrapolation)
outputs.interpretation: This multiplies the combined per-patient cost (in 2000 dollars) by a selectable national reported case count to illustrate how a nationwide total scales. The document's own stated nationwide estimate (~$203 million) is expressed in 2002 dollars using the 2002 case count of 23,763; this computed value will not exactly match that figure because an apparent additional 2000-to-2002 dollar adjustment in the document's own calculation is not reproduced here. This is a regional, clinically defined cohort's cost scaled to a national surveillance-defined case count - two different case definitions and years - and the document's authors note the surveillance count is believed to undercount true nationwide Lyme disease burden.
